findings.text: The same crushing verb is used destructively of enemies and redemptively of the self, with no lexical marker distinguishing the two. H1792 and H1794 (dakha, dakhah, to crush) are applied, in the same handful of verses, destructively, of enemies and oppressors crushed in judgment (you crushed Rahab like a carcass, Ps 89:10; crush the oppressor, Ps 72:4; the wicked who crush your people, Ps 94:5), and redemptively, of the self, as the state God desires and does not despise (a broken and contrite heart, Ps 51:17; him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, Isa 57:15), where crushed names the humbled disposition that draws God near. The Niphal and Pual senses of H1792 include both to be crushed and to be contrite in one entry; only the referent, an enemy or one's own heart, tells which reading applies.

findings.text: H2555 (chamas, violence, 43 verses) is the family's real anchor, structural and social and not incidental: it defines violence as a filled-world condition rather than isolated acts. The paradigm case is the pre-Flood indictment, the earth was filled with violence (Gen 6:11, 6:13); the recurring pattern afterward is social and structural: false witness (Ps 27:12, Exod 23:1), dishonest commerce and oppression of the poor (Ps 12:5, Amos 3:10), and a garment of violence worn by the wicked as a visible attribute (Ps 73:6, Ezek 7:23).
Isaiah 53:9, he had done no violence, uses this same word (chamas) as the Servant's negative self-defence, converging with Isaiah 53:10's crushing verb (dakha, the same family) in the same Song.

This is the fifth family in the exercise to converge independently on Isaiah 53 (after guilt, transgression, iniquity and the bearing verb nasa): the convergence is now a five-family pattern (D, F, G and the guilt subgroup's H0817 and H5375J), so this Servant passage functions as a hub text across the M10 cluster's vocabulary, worth flagging as a standalone pattern and a cross-family note rather than being rediscovered in each family's synthesis.

nodes.disposition_note: the lines name Isaiah 53 as a whole chapter; the family's own verses in the Song are 53:9 and 53:10
